Twenty-four comments

The Falcarragh

From the playing of the young Clare band “Turas”. Apparently this is a composition of guitar player Alphie Duggan, probably best known as Tommy Peoples’ accompanist on “The Quiet Glen”. It’s one of those hornpipes that sounds more like a slow reel. Nice tune, it’s taken me a while to get round to posting it.

OK, it’s official. My name is Jason and I’m addicted to this tune. There. I said it.

Nice mode

I like the second part. G-lidian a very rare mode in irish music.

↳ Posted by Osher on September 1st, 2007.

It is indeed rare. But this isn’t in G lydian, it’s in G major with some C# accidentals, which is very common in Irish music. That’s an important distinction, especially for backers.

Re: The Falcarragh

This is indeed my tune.
The version here is of course not entirely accurate, but the process of passing it around has not dis-improved it imho. That notwithstanding, I have to insist that in the turn the second C is a natural, moving from the previous C#, with repetitions following suit.
The only recorded version I have heard is that by my old mate Martin Nolan and he cast it in D which makes a beautiful version that I would never have originated.
It’s a fact that Trad tunes are not readily amenable to picking on the standard-tuned guitar and this tune was a slightly mischievous attempt to produce one that would be easy on the guitar and difficult on e.g. the fiddle, while retaining the necessary elements to appeal to the traditional ear. The fact that I have heard it played back to me so many times indicates that it has had a certain success.
I’m surprised and delighted to see it turning up on thesession.org

Re: The Falcarragh

In response to birlibirdie (I’m not an inhabitor of thesession.org and only today realised that I could get an email if a comment appeared here - please forgive any unintentional rudeness) I mentioned earlier that from a guitarist perspective (standard tuning) traditional reels, jigs etc are inclined to be unfriendly when it comes to picking them. With a back-pocket code that I would never accompany a tune that I could not pick (or at least lilt) it meant a lot of (enjoyable) hassle picking through O’Neill’s (or whatever). I began to realise (reference the mandolin) that tunes were a lot more (I’m going to say) shapely on the fiddle and it occurred to me to wonder what might be handy on the guitar but would pose a challenge on the fiddle.

The opening phrase of the Falcarragh was what occurred to me. It had a hornpipe feel about it and the first part came very easily. Around that time I had had an in-depth and up-close experience with a troupe of dancers and was particularly impressed with their slow (hard shoe) hornpipes so all I did was imagine someone dancing a slow hornpipe and the tune just flowed. I’d love to hear someone dancing to it (but I do hear it as a very slow tune, with lots of intricate footwork and room for it).

Shortly after that I found myself up in Falcarragh trying to improve my Gaeilge but with time on my hands. The second part took a little while. Again the driving thought was simplicity on the guitar and I was concerned that what I came up with could be considered (on other instruments (and particularly the fiddle (it’s a bit of knuckle-cruncher))) to be more trouble than it was worth. But I had been asked to contribute to a small concert and on the night decided that I might as well play this new piece. As I introduced it I thought it might do its reception no harm if I said (as Gaeilge) that I proposed to call it the Falcarragh hornpipe. That worked and people were very kind.

Others to whom I played it were similarly kind and I remember various people learning it, particularly Pat Gough on concertina. When I moved to Clare I passed it on to a few people including the wonderful but sadly departed Dympna O’Sullivan (again concertina). Marcus Moloney, ace banjo, learnt it and it was recorded by a group he was in - he will sometimes launch into it when he sees me sneaking in to wherever he’s playing.

The tune now has a life of its own and turns up in my life periodically. It changes all the time but seems to survive in its essence. Most ironically I was at Willie Week pipering classes a few years back when teacher decided we should all learn Alph’s lovely tune. In G! On the pipes! Hoist by my own petard….

I don’t know how to upload notation to this site or I might have a go at offering the original (but not necessarily the best) version.

Thanks for the interest and I hope that’s not a bore.

Re: The Falcarragh

How tunes are composed or write themselves, how they morph and acquire a life of their own is a fascinating subject indeed.
In your story here, the details about the relationship to the dance are especially precious I think. How both the presence of the dancers and the very idea of the dance -the steps, the ‘slow’, intricate footwork- translated into a musical picture, at least partially, for you.

And I agree; the slower this hornpipe is played, the better.
If I may add: tonight offered an unforeseen illustration of it for me for I was doodling with The Falcarragh for a good while on a friend’s guitar and he said it reminded him of Satyajit Ray’s The Music Room (!). He tends to be sarcastic and I thought he was taking the piss but he was actually serious. He’d seen that film years before. So I played it more and I heard what he heard and tried to go further with it: playing this hornpipe in D (drop D tuning) rather slowly made it acquire a depth I did not suspect. It kept me going for an hour or more. To be true, I wove in modal intervals that were not in the original but the fact remained: what I was playing was at all times recognizably the Falcarragh Hornpipe. A very dependable tune then!
Best of luck to it and its progenitor!

The Falcarragh, X:5

At last the (unimproved) original. I haven’t used the conventional ‘dotted’ hornpipe notation because that’s not what it’s supposed to sound like - but it should be played with swing (which means that every two half-notes should be played as if they were the first and third notes of a triplet (so an underlying rhythm of ‘diddly diddly’)).

My apologies for intruding an original composition into this wonderful site (contrary to site policy (I know)) but since it got here before me I hope that I might perhaps be forgiven just this once. Fingers crossed…

↳ Posted by Alph Duggan on July 11th, 2023.

The Falcarragh, X:6

A hopefully-not-too-intrusive “improvement” on Alph’s surely not intrusive unimproved improvement (help! I’m lost). Could an idiosyncratic 12/8 hornpipe solution posted on the 12/7 really prove an improvement on the unimproved tune setting situation or simply plain confusing? Could the 12/8 audio actually improve the learning experience of the idiotic learners who cannot-will not read music and still think they can learn the Falcarragh like true dotted-quaver-hornpipe score-reading heroes? I humbly hope so.
Progress may be hopeless but, actually, I just wanted to experience the trill of the chase for the perfect version by posting yet another imperfect setting! Let not the sun set on anyone’s resentment for, plainly, whether this tune is played plainly ‘improved’ or simply ‘unimproved’ -if a little adorned still-, it’s great. I like it. So please excuse my manners. It’s late.

↳ Posted by Alph Duggan on April 29th, 2024.

Re: The Falcarragh

👍
Indeed they are.
Visual scores lean one way; audios lean another; rhythmically, melodically, timbre wise, keys-wise…
This site’s main aim is to help musicians of any capacity decypher and make sense of tunes. Any change of angle can help in this endeavour. Hence the 12/8 above.
One thing teachers notice in their practice is how easily students can acquire a phrase or a notion once deemed difficult when a different approach is suggested. The difference in the approach can be slight but the result huge.
A multiple angle approach helps with memory and helps refine musical gestures as well.
As a teacher I use it increasingly systematically; it gives students a sense of freedom and reponsiblity, both, when they practice shifting / changing the meter, key, tempo, fingering, etc of a given tune.
